blocks.content: J&K's demography chapter must be handled with particular factual care given its sensitivity — this chapter presents population, religious composition, and the historically significant Kashmiri Pandit displacement as neutrally stated facts, without attributing motive or taking a side in ongoing political debate.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Jammu & Kashmir presents a diverse demographic structure with distinct regional majorities in Jammu, Kashmir, and Ladakh.
The Jammu & Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020 recognized five official languages: Kashmiri, Dogri, Urdu, Hindi, and English.
The year 1990 marked the severe internal displacement and mass exodus of the Kashmiri Pandit minority from the Kashmir Valley.
Kashmiri and Dogri are the major regional spoken languages included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The most recent decennial Census figures available for J&K remain from 2011 (the 2021 Census was deferred nationally); when quoting these figures for the present-day UT specifically, remember they cover the combined erstwhile state INCLUDING areas now in Ladakh UT, so exact present-day J&K-UT-only figures are necessarily estimates pending a fresh Census.
The mass exodus of the Kashmiri Pandit community in 1990 significantly altered the demographic landscape of the Kashmir Valley.

items: The Kashmir Valley has a large Muslim majority population (predominantly Sunni, with a smaller Shia minority, notably in areas such as Budgam); the Jammu division has a Hindu-majority population overall, though with significant Muslim-majority pockets in border districts such as Poonch and Rajouri; Ladakh (now a separate UT) has a roughly balanced Buddhist-majority (Leh district) and Muslim-majority (Kargil district) population split.

Sikh and Christian minorities are present in smaller numbers across both divisions, with Sikh communities historically concentrated in parts of both Jammu and the Kashmir Valley, including a small but historically significant Kashmiri Sikh population.

This regional-religious diversity across Jammu, Kashmir and (formerly) Ladakh has been a persistent factor in the region's political dynamics, including debates over the appropriate balance of representation and resources between the divisions — a theme touched on in Chapter 16's discussion of the 2022 delimitation exercise.

blocks.content: Kashmiri Pandits are the Hindu Brahmin community historically native to the Kashmir Valley, forming a small but culturally and historically significant minority within the Valley's population prior to 1990.

Beginning in early 1990, amid the onset of the armed insurgency described in Chapter 12, a large majority of the Kashmiri Pandit community left the Valley over a short period, in circumstances that included targeted killings of some community members, threats, and a climate of acute insecurity — resulting in a mass displacement that fundamentally altered the Valley's demographic and social composition and remains, more than three decades later, an unresolved and deeply significant chapter in the region's contemporary social history.

Most displaced Kashmiri Pandit families have since resided in Jammu, Delhi and other parts of India, with various government rehabilitation and return-and-resettlement schemes (including efforts to build secure residential colonies within the Valley for returning families, and reserved government employment provisions) implemented over the years with varying degrees of uptake and continuing debate over their adequacy; the 5 nominated Assembly seats for displaced persons (Chapter 16) are one specific representational response to this displacement.

This subject remains genuinely sensitive and actively debated — including differing views on the precise causes, extent, and appropriate remedies for the displacement — and candidates should treat it as an important, factually well-documented historical event while avoiding one-sided characterisations in exam answers.

★ EXAM POINT: The Kashmiri Pandit exodus (from early 1990) is a certain-to-be-tested demographic/historical fact — state it factually (community, approximate date, scale of displacement, and the existence of ongoing rehabilitation efforts) without over-claiming precise figures or attributing detailed motive, since exact statistics and causal accounts vary across sources.

items: J&K Official Languages Act, 2020: Remember that Kashmiri, Dogri, and Hindi were added alongside traditional official languages Urdu and English.
Census 2011 figures for J&K: Sex ratio of 889 females per 1000 males and overall literacy rate of 67.16%.
Eighth Schedule Languages: Note that Dogri was added via the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

Kashmiri is the majority language of the Kashmir Valley, written traditionally in the Perso-Arabic script (though also written in Sharada and Devanagari scripts in different contexts) and belonging to the Dardic sub-group of the Indo-Aryan language family.

Dogri is the majority language of the Jammu division's plains areas, and — significant as a national-level fact — was added to the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution in 2003, granting it official recognised-language status at the national level.

Urdu has historically served as the erstwhile state's (and now the UT's) official administrative language, alongside Hindi and English in wider use; other locally significant languages include Gojri (spoken by the Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoral communities), Pahari, and Ladakhi/Bhoti (predominantly in the now-separate Ladakh UT).

In 2020, the Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020 added Kashmiri, Dogri and Hindi as additional official languages of the UT alongside the pre-existing Urdu and English, reflecting a significant post-2019 linguistic-policy change explicitly aimed at giving greater official recognition to the region's major indigenous languages.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020 (making Kashmiri, Dogri, Hindi, Urdu and English all official languages of the UT) is a frequently tested post-2019 policy change — a five-language official framework, a significant expansion from the earlier Urdu-centric arrangement.

items: Combined erstwhile state population (2011): approx 1.25 crore; sex ratio approx 889/1000; literacy approx 67-68%.
Kashmir Valley: Muslim-majority; Jammu division: Hindu-majority overall (with Muslim-majority border pockets like Poonch, Rajouri).
Kashmiri Pandit exodus began early 1990, a major and sensitive demographic/historical event; 5 nominated Assembly seats partly address displaced-persons representation.
Kashmiri (Dardic, Indo-Aryan) = majority language of the Valley; Dogri = majority language of Jammu plains, added to the Constitution's Eighth Schedule in 2003.
J&K Official Languages Act, 2020: Kashmiri, Dogri, Hindi, Urdu and English are all now official languages of the UT.
